From @C_Barraud’s packed Monday Morning Brief, @AndreasSteno says “Everything is upside down to the dot com pricing.”

Two of the valuation items in the brief (the second from @MikeZaccardi via @yardeni):

▪️ In March 2000, S&P tech traded at 55x and Cisco at 130x, while Staples sat at 17x. Today, as I mentioned last week, the Nasdaq-100 is at about 18x, the lowest since the Covid crash. Nvidia is at 11x and Micron at 4x, while Walmart and Costco trade at 40x and 42x.
▪️ Consumer Staples’ forward P/E has climbed to 24.2x, the highest since 1999. That’s well above its 5-year (20.8x) and 10-year (20.1x) averages.

Goldman’s thematic desk was already leaning against the move last week. As I noted in that week’s Week Ahead (https://t.co/JZ7uYgRz4o), it liked shorting its Staples basket, which had beaten the S&P 500 by nearly 20% over the prior month. They noted similar metrics:

▪️ S&P Staples’ valuation premium to the index is the highest in more than 10 years.
▪️ The basket’s 2.84% dividend yield is 2.05pp below the 10-year Treasury yield, the 1st percentile of the last 10 years.
▪️ Historically, Staples have lagged over the next three months after similar runs, except in late 2021/early 2022.

Looking at the charts, on Nov 5, $XLP’s one-month lead over $SPY hit +18.4%. Only April and October 2000 and March 2020 were higher. Since 1999 there have been 10 earlier runs of 12% or more, and XLP lagged over the next three months in 6 of them (median −4.5%).

The exceptions: 2000 (twice), late 2008 and 2022. Each came during an S&P 500 bear market that kept grinding lower over the next three months. Being in a bear market wasn’t enough on its own though: the 2001 and March 2020 runs also came during bear markets, and Staples lagged as stocks bounced. So the short is really a bet on a rebound.

Even if it is a 2000 replay, the starting point is very different. Staples went into the dot-com unwind at 17x. They’re going into this one at 24x.

Looking at the seasonality breakdown from @AlmanacTrader, editor of the Stock Trader’s Almanac & Almanac Investor Newsletter, this week we hit the low point of November’s mid-month dip, with the caveat that we haven’t done a very good job of following the seasonal pattern so far this month (more on that in a minute).

In midterm years, Tuesday (day 12) has brought the sharpest drop. The Nasdaq has fallen about 0.8%, the Russell 2000 about 0.7%, the S&P 500 and Russell 1000 about 0.5%, and the DJIA about 0.45%. Hirsch flags the same day for small caps across all years: the Russell 2000 has risen on the 12th trading day just 12 times in the last 42 years, averaging −0.39%. The midterm lines bottom by Wednesday and rebound Thursday and Friday, leaving the week down about 0.15–0.3%.

Friday is also monthly options expiration, which falls in the week before Thanksgiving this year. Hirsch notes the DJIA rose in this week ten straight years from 1993 to 2002 and has been up in 21 of the last 33, but it has been down in seven of the last nine. Expiration day itself has a bullish bias, with the DJIA up 17 of the last 24, though five of the declines have come in the last ten years. The 21-year averages fit that recent record: the week is down, but Friday is up.

From the day-14 low, the strong finish in Hirsch’s pattern takes over, with every index rallying through Thanksgiving week into month-end.

As noted, though, November is lagging the typical seasonal pattern. The S&P 500 is down 0.2% for the month through day 10 (from −2.7% through day 5), and the Nasdaq-100 1.6% (from −4.9%), versus 21-year average gains of roughly 0.7%–1.2% for the major indices by this point (about 1.8%–2.3% in midterm years), again reinforcing that seasonality is just a general guide to how markets have historically performed, certainly not a prediction of how they will actually perform.

Banks don't lend reserves. They lever reserves and make IOUs on top of them, rather than "creating money."

But then whenever those IOUs start to fail at scale, the central bank creates more reserves for them.

Over the past 50 years, if the US central bank held reserves flat and banks kept making money, there'd be a 160-to-1 ratio between deposits and reserves, which would be untenable. However, whenever it comes even slightly untenable, the central bank creates more reserves and swaps them for assets from banks, boosting the ratio and giving banks more lending/leveraging ability to keep it growing.

The US bank deposit-to-reserve ratio is under 4-to-1 because the central bank accommodates bank lending by creating new reserves.

A good man with power can fix bad men with power for about 30 years or so. And even a good man usually grows more corrupt and detached over decades.

To more persistently fix a bad situation after defeating it historically requires putting in place a more durable institution that is not tied to a single, centralized, person. And that requires cultivating buy-in by the population to support that institution more-so than the person.

This goes all the way back to why humans and other apes are different. Apes recognize a singular ape as having power, which works at the scale of the jungle. Humans can abstract the position of the leader ape, the leader human, from the individual currently in charge, and ask what process should we follow for rulership and law in a long-term sense to inhabit that position. We have the mental capacity to separate the position from the person. What rules do we follow that are broader than one person, to lead to rulership from generation to generation?

Sometimes a key man is needed (or a woman, usually a man, let's say person) for change when things are dire. But what turns a temporary change into a durable institution is whether they can land the plane in a way that carries on beyond them.

Can they gain power and then distribute it? Can they become the ape that dominates the other apes and then separates himself from that position, so that what was built can continue on for centuries?

Most don't. Most continue the cycle of emerging markets that never emerge. Rarely, one bubbles to the top and manages it, in a context to more durably transfer leadership, transfer law, and signal to the world that the rule of law and rule of capital in their country isn't tied to one person but rather has a broader base to bet on. That base requires citizens to buy into it, and for their leaders to empower independent courts. It's less about one leader at that point, and more about whether the culture that let bad men come into power is now more durably able to put good men (and women) in power or not. What changed, culturally and legally? What was put in place to stop the cycle? To make the centralized power not tied to one mortal person, but rather able to transfer? What turned chaos into law for more than one lifetime?

The narrow path is to win decisively, and then help distribute the power, and teach the new culture. But few manage it. It's like rising to a George Washington level of domination and then gradually letting go.

Bitcoin is a volatile asset, which means taking the lumps. Here are my thoughts on the game of chicken that is investing in the accelerating debt-debasement era.

Last week's fall was a 3.4 sigma vol-adjusted move, #21 of 299 since 2014.

In August, I said the breakout was unlikely to fail. But it always happened against a late liquidity-cycle setup, where debt growth > liquidity growth.

What matters now is where the fall happened and how liquidity drivers move.

Above my market regime filter, falls like this were higher 6 months later 8 of 9 times. Below it, where we are now, 10 of 17 (median +2%). Statistically, the skew is to the downside. 

But it's the same message as February's capitulation near $60K: this is a value zone. Boring as it sounds, idle capital should see this as an opportunity. Another leg down, if it comes, would be a gift; key levels are realised price and long-term holder cost at around ~$53k & ~$48k, respectively. These levels aren't FUD; there is an air pocket below $60k based on onchain cost levels. 

On-chain, this looks more like a shakeout than capitulation. Recent buyers are selling at a loss but long-term holders aren't (LTH-SOPR ~1.0 vs 0.4-0.7 at cycle lows), and 30-day realised losses are a tenth of February's.

Flipside, a weekly close above ~$73K reclaims my trend-regime filter, and ~$75k reclaims short-term holder cost basis. That's only 15% above here and within the bounds of pure noise. The point is that price is wedged tight between key levels. 

The trigger is the macro drivers turning. They're going the wrong way but could be near exhaustion. I say near, but nothing is definitive until the DXY reverses. $BTC inflections are typically signalled by dollar reversals. 

My expectation is the definitive liquidity low in 2027. Bitcoin should bottom before it. Unless it's completely delinked from global liquidity (it's at its lowest in the modern era), which I do not believe; the August Bessent buyback announcement is a good indication: when liquidity turns, Bitcoin will outperform every other asset.

I suspect 2027 is when they will be forced to swerve again. Every regime is different; liquidity mechanisms morph out of necessity. We are late stage in the global debt & debasement game. And owning Bitcoin is always a game of chicken with the central planners.
